claims.text: Strength in multi-component concentrated alloys is governed by interactions of dislocations with solute atoms and precipitates.
Deformation or failure behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys is governed by interactions of dislocations with solute atoms and precipitates.
Aging precipitates solute atoms from the solution-treated and quenched alloy.
Dislocation density and distribution are structural mediators of the aging response.
Dislocation-solute interactions contribute to the governing mechanism.
Dislocation-precipitate interactions contribute to the governing mechanism.
Increasing aging time increases strength relative to the solution-treated and quenched baseline.
Increasing aging time decreases ductility relative to the solution-treated and quenched baseline.
The proposed behavior applies from 20 to 500 degrees Celsius.
The proposed behavior applies at strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1.
Beyond an unspecified aging time, over-aging occurs.
The hypothesis predicts that strength should decrease with increasing aging time.
The hypothesis predicts that dislocation density or distribution should change with aging.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says strength increases with aging time, whereas the falsification rule treats failure of strength to decrease with aging time as falsifying, implying the opposite expected direction.

The predicted outcome states that strength increases with increasing aging time without limiting that trend, while the boundary states that strength decreases after over-aging. The intended non-monotonic trend is not reconciled with a specified aging-time regime.
